say: You give it a function, $f(x)$. It gives back the **inverse**, $f^{-1}(x)$, the function that undoes $f$.
The key idea: $f$ takes $x$ to $y$, so its inverse takes $y$ back to $x$. Swap the letters $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$.

how.higher: Higher level asks it on Paper 1 as a 5-mark part (2016, 2018), once as the last step after showing a function is bijective and once as the inverse of a cubic.

example.question: The function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by $f(x) = \frac{3x + 4}{2}$. $f$ is bijective. Find $f^{-1}(x)$.

steps.title: Write f as y
steps.say: Replace $f(x)$ with $y$. This is the rule that takes $x$ to $y$.

steps.title: Swap x and y
steps.say: The inverse takes $y$ back to $x$, so swap the two letters. Now $\hl{1}{y}$ is the output we want.

steps.title: Solve for y
steps.say: Rearrange to get $\hl{1}{y}$ on its own. Clear the fraction first.

steps.title: Name the inverse
steps.say: This $y$ is the inverse function. Write it as $f^{-1}(x)$.

higher.tip: Say why the inverse exists: a function is bijective if its inverse exists. Writing $f^{-1}(x)$ in part (i) is already work of merit.

sources.quote: Function is bijective if inverse exists

higher.tip: Rearranging the formula for $x$ in terms of $y$ earns partial credit even if you slip afterwards.
For an inverse found from points, getting two image points right earns partial credit. Swap the coordinates of each point carefully.

say: You give it the graph of a function $f$. It draws the graph of its inverse, $f^{-1}$.
The key idea: the inverse swaps $x$ and $y$, so every point $(a, b)$ on $f$ becomes $(b, a)$. That is a **reflection** in the line $y = x$.

how.higher: Higher level asks it on Paper 1 (2018, 2025): a 5-mark part giving the inverse of a function from its graph, and a 15-mark question where the graph of $g^{-1}$ is drawn on a given diagram.

example.question: The graph of $f(x) = 2^x$ is shown. Sketch the graph of $f^{-1}$ by reflecting in the line $y = x$, and write down $f^{-1}(x)$.

steps.title: Pick points on f
steps.say: Read three points off the graph of $f$. Use easy ones.

steps.title: Swap the coordinates
steps.say: A reflection in $y = x$ swaps $x$ and $y$. Each point $(a, b)$ becomes $(b, a)$.

steps.title: Draw and label
steps.say: Draw the line $y = x$, plot the new points and join them with a smooth curve. Label it $f^{-1}$. The curve never touches the $y$-axis.

lines.text: The inverse of $2^x$ is the **log** to base $2$.

higher.tip: Label your inverse graph. A correct curve with no label loses a mark.
Show your work on the diagram itself, with lines or marks on the graph. Answers with no work shown lose a mark.
Plotting just two correct image points of the reflection earns partial credit.

say: You give it a log function like $\log_2 x$. It draws the **log curve**.
The key idea: $y = \log_a x$ means $x = a^y$. So it is the graph of $a^x$ reflected in $y = x$: choose $y$, work out $x$, plot $(x, y)$.

how.higher: Higher level asks it on Paper 1 (2018) inside a 20-mark modelling question, where a table of values for a log-based function is completed and plotted.

example.question: Draw the graph of $y = \log_2 x$ for $\frac{1}{4} \le x \le 8$. Use a table of values.

steps.title: Change to index form
steps.say: A log is hard to evaluate for chosen $x$. Turn it into index form: $y = \log_2 x$ means $x = 2^y$.

steps.title: Choose y, find x
steps.say: Pick whole numbers for $\hl{1}{y}$ and work out $x$.

steps.title: Plot and join
steps.say: Plot $(x, y)$ for each pair and join the points with a smooth curve. It rises slowly and never reaches the $y$-axis.

higher.tip: Fill the table first. Even one correct entry earns partial credit.
Plot every value from your own table. Plots that match your table still earn marks, as long as at least one table value is right.

sources.quote: All plots consistent with candidates table

higher.tip: A correct table with wrong plots still earns high partial credit, so take care with the plotting.

say: You give it a function $f(x)$ and a point $a$. It finds the **limit**, the value $f(x)$ gets close to as $x$ gets close to $a$, and tells you if the function is continuous there.
The key idea: the limit does not need $f(a)$ to exist. If putting in $a$ gives $\frac{0}{0}$, simplify first, then put in $a$.

steps.title: Try substituting
steps.say: Put $x = 5$ straight in. If it fails, we need to simplify.

lines.text: The bottom is $5 - 5 = 0$ too, so we get $\frac{0}{0}$. That means nothing yet.

steps.title: Factorise the top
steps.say: The top is a quadratic, so factorise it. Look for a factor $(x - 5)$ to cancel.

steps.title: Cancel and substitute
steps.say: For $x \ne 5$ the $(x - 5)$ cancels. The limit only cares about $x$ near $5$, not at $5$. Put $x = 5$ into what is left.

steps.title: Check continuity
steps.say: Continuous at $5$ needs $f(5)$ to exist and to equal the limit.

lines.text: $f(5) = \frac{0}{0}$ is not defined, so $f$ is **not continuous** at $x = 5$.
The limit $\hl{1}{7}$ exists, but there is a gap in the graph at $x = 5$.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{limit} = 7;\ f \text{ is not continuous at } x = 5
